## Overview

Over the last couple weeks you built a species distribution model (SDM) that shows where the climate suits your species now and where it is projected to suit it in the future. But a map of future suitable habitat doesn't tell you whether the species can actually *get there*. That is the third part of your capstone: an evaluation of how your species will move from where it is now to where it will need to be. For your final paper, you won't have to run and report the actual analysis (it requires a qualitative evaluation only), but this lab will help you think of how we describe linkages between suitable habitat patches. 

This week you'll use your Lab 10 SDM to design a corridor. The steps are:

1. Define where the species is now and where it needs to go (patches of suitable habitat)
2. Convert relative environmental suitability into a **resistance surface**
3. Find the **least-cost path** and a **least-cost corridor** between the patches
4. Evaluate the corridor, including how adding human development changes it, and decide how far to trust it

A few definitions:

- **Resistance** is how much a landscape hinders movement, so a cell with high resistance is costly to cross. 
- **Least-cost path** is the single cheapest route between two locations, found by adding up the resistance of the cells along each possible route. 
- **Least-cost corridor** is a band of cells whose combined cost is close to the cheapest possible, so it shows several near-best routes rather than a single line.

Zeller et al. (2012), which you read for lecture, reviewed several ways to estimate resistance. In this lab we use the approach based on habitat suitability, which assumes that the places animals prefer are also the places they find easy to move through. As you saw in lecture and in the reading, that assumption isn't always true: use is not the same as movement, and dispersing animals often behave differently from residents. Keep that in mind as you work. The corridor you produce is a hypothesis, not a prediction.

I'll use the San Joaquin kit fox as the example, as in Lab 10. You can, and probably should, use the outputs from your own species' SDM instead. If you didn't use your project species in the previous lab, you could try asking someone from your group very nicely to use their lab 10 outputs. Otherwise, the kit fox output files are in the Lab 10 files folder on Canvas.

To help you envision what the outputs should look like, I will be uploading a knitted version of my kit fox lab with plots and outputs included to the assignment page on Canvas. You can reference that to make sure you're on the right track.

### Learning Outcomes
After completing this lab, you should be able to:

1. Define source and destination patches from current and future suitability maps
2. Convert relative environmental suitability into a resistance surface using a negative exponential transformation
3. Calculate a least-cost path and a least-cost corridor with `leastcostpath`
4. Add a human footprint layer to a resistance surface and evaluate how it changes the corridor
5. Interpret the corridor and describe its limitations


## Getting started: Load your SDM outputs

At the end of Lab 10, you saved three files in your working folder: `suitability_current.tif`, `suitability_future.tif` (relative environmental suitability from your best model, for current and 2041-2060 climate, on the same grid), and `occurrence_points.csv` (your occurrence records). If you didn't save them, you can use the kit fox files posted on Canvas (look in the Lab 10 folder under Files).

```{r load-data}
current.suit <- rast("suitability_current.tif")
future.suit  <- rast("suitability_future.tif")
names(current.suit) <- "suitability"
names(future.suit)  <- "suitability"

occ <- read.csv("occurrence_points.csv")
occ.vect <- vect(occ, geom = c("x", "y"), crs = "epsg:4326")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(current.suit, main = "Current", range = c(0, 1))
plot(future.suit, main = "Future (2041-2060)", range = c(0, 1))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

global(current.suit, "range", na.rm = TRUE)
global(future.suit, "range", na.rm = TRUE)
```

### Projecting to meters

These maps are in latitude/longitude. Least-cost analysis adds up the cost of moving between neighboring cells, so it needs a projected coordinate system with units of meters (and the `leastcostpath` package requires one). We'll project both maps to UTM, as in Lab 10, at a cell size of 4 km (about the size of the original cells). If your species is in a different part of the world, choose a projected CRS appropriate for your study area.

```{r project}
proj.crs <- "epsg:32610
"

current.proj <- project(current.suit, proj.crs, res = 4000, method = "bilinear")

# project the future map onto exactly the same grid as the current map
future.proj  <- project(future.suit, current.proj, method = "bilinear")

res(current.proj)
dim(current.proj)
```

## Defining patches: where the species is now, and where it needs to go

A least-cost path connects two locations, so we need to decide what those are. We'll do this in three steps.

**1. Decide what counts as "suitable."** The SDM gives a continuous index, so we need a threshold. A common choice is the suitability value that includes 90% of your occurrence records (the 10th percentile of suitability at the occurrence points). Cells at or above that value are "suitable."

```{r threshold}
occ.proj <- project(occ.vect, proj.crs)
occ.suit <- extract(current.proj, occ.proj, ID = FALSE)[, 1]  # extract suitability values at every occ point

threshold <- as.numeric(quantile(occ.suit, probs = 0.10, na.rm = TRUE))
cat("threshold 1: ", threshold)

threshold2 <- as.numeric(quantile(occ.suit, probs = 0.30, na.rm = TRUE))
cat("threshold 2: ", threshold2)

```



**2. Find the patches.** We identify the suitable cells in the current and future maps, then use `patches()` to group neighboring suitable cells into numbered patches. 

```{r patches, fig.width=10}
current.suitable <- ifel(current.proj >= threshold, 1, NA)
future.suitable  <- ifel(future.proj  >= threshold, 1, NA)


current.suitable2 <- ifel(current.proj >= threshold2, 1, NA)
future.suitable2  <- ifel(future.proj  >= threshold2, 1, NA)

# New (2x2)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(current.suitable, main = "Current [90% Occ]", range = c(0, 1))
plot(future.suitable, main = "Future (2041-2060) [90% Occ]", range = c(0, 1))
plot(current.suitable2, main = "Current [70% Occ]", range = c(0, 1))
plot(future.suitable2, main = "Future (2041-2060) [70% Occ]", range = c(0, 1))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Let's just use the first threshold
current.patches <- patches(current.suitable, directions = 8)
plot(current.patches, main = "Current patches")


# calculate the size of each current patch, in km2
patch.sizes <- freq(current.patches)
patch.sizes$area.km2 <- patch.sizes$count * prod(res(current.proj)) / 1e6
head(patch.sizes)
```


We also find the **gain** areas: cells that are suitable in the future but not now. These are the places your species will need to reach.
```{r gain}
# which areas show future suitability but are not in the current 'suitable' map?
gain <- ifel(future.proj >= threshold & current.proj < threshold, 1, NA)
n.gain <- global(gain, "notNA")[1, 1]     # how many cells are gain area?
n.gain
plot(gain, main = "New future habitat")

# plot combined
plot(current.suitable, main = "Current vs Gain", range = c(0, 1),legend=F)
plot(gain,col="green",legend=F,add=T)
terra::add_legend("topright",legend=c("Current","Gain"),fill=c("yellow","green"))

```


If `n.gain` is 0, your species is projected to gain no new area, and you should skip the next chunk and use the "No gain area?" chunk below it instead.

```{r gain-patches}
gain.patches <- patches(gain, directions = 8)
plot(gain.patches, main = "Future new patches")

gain.sizes <- freq(gain.patches)
gain.sizes$area.km2 <- gain.sizes$count * prod(res(current.proj)) / 1e6
head(gain.sizes)
```

```{r no-gain, eval=FALSE}
# ONLY use this chunk if your species has no gain area. Instead of connecting a current patch to a
# new area, connect the two largest FUTURE patches (the future refuges):
future.patches <- patches(future.suitable, directions = 8)
future.sizes <- freq(future.patches)
future.sizes <- future.sizes[order(future.sizes$count, decreasing = TRUE), ]

# then, in the "source and destination" chunk below, use future.patches in place of
# current.patches (source = future.sizes$value[1]) and in place of gain.patches (destination = future.sizes$value[2])
```



**3. Pick one location to represent each patch.** We'll connect the **largest current patch** (the source) to the **largest gain patch** (the destination), using the highest-suitability cell in each as the starting and ending points. Using one point per patch is a simplification, which we'll come back to in Exercise 5. The function below finds that best cell; a function is just a reusable set of instructions, like the ones you've been calling from packages.

```{r nodes}
# find the location of the highest-suitability cell within the given patch(es)
get.best.cells <- function(patch.raster, suit.raster, patch.ids) {
  xy <- NULL
  for (id in patch.ids) {
    cells <- ifel(patch.raster == id, suit.raster, NA)
    idx <- which.max(values(cells)[, 1])
    xy <- rbind(xy, xyFromCell(cells, idx))
  }
  xy
}  # after running this, the function you defined is now stored in your environment, and you can use it on your data

src.id  <- patch.sizes$value[which.max(patch.sizes$count)]   # Which current patch is largest?
dest.id <- gain.sizes$value[which.max(gain.sizes$count)]     # Which future gained patch is largest?

src.xy  <- get.best.cells(current.patches, current.proj, src.id)   # using the function you defined above
dest.xy <- get.best.cells(gain.patches, future.proj, dest.id)

src.xy
dest.xy
```

## From suitability to resistance

Now we convert suitability into resistance. A simple option is a straight line: resistance = 1 − suitability. But Keeley et al. (2016) found, for long-distance movers, that a *negative exponential* transformation worked better. The idea is that animals will readily move through moderately suitable habitat and avoid only the worst. The transformation is:

$$
R = 100 - 99 \times \frac{1 - e^{-c \, h}}{1 - e^{-c}}
$$

where *R* is resistance (from 1, the best habitat, to 100, the worst), *h* is suitability (0 to 1), and *c* controls the shape of the curve. When c is about 0.25, the relationship is nearly a straight line. As *c* increases, resistance drops quickly as suitability rises, so most of the landscape becomes easy to cross. We'll use c = 4, a commonly used value for mobile species. Let's see what that curve looks like:

```{r resistance, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
# the shape of the transformation
h <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
plot(h, 100 - 99 * ((1 - exp(-4 * h)) / (1 - exp(-4))), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Suitability", ylab = "Resistance")
lines(h, 100 - 99 * ((1 - exp(-0.25 * h)) / (1 - exp(-0.25))), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("c = 4", "c = 0.25"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2)

plot(h, 100 - 99 * ((1 - exp(-10 * h)) / (1 - exp(-10))), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Suitability", ylab = "Resistance")
```

The `leastcostpath` package works with **conductance**, the opposite of resistance: higher values mean easier movement. So we take the inverse of resistance and build the cost surface (the output of `create_cs` is referred to as a 'conductanceMatrix'). Using 16 neighbors means a path can move in 16 directions from each cell, which makes paths less "blocky" than using 4 or 8.

```{r cost-surface, fig.width=10}
c.par <- 6
# generate resistance surface
resistance <- 100 - 99 * ((1 - exp(-c.par * future.proj)) / (1 - exp(-c.par)))

# transform to conductance surface
conductance <- 1 / resistance

# generate the cost surface
cs <- create_cs(x = conductance, neighbours = 16)

par(mfrow=c(1,3))
plot(resistance, main = "Resistance")
plot(conductance, main = "Conductance")
plot(cs, main = "Cost Surface")
par(mfrow=c(1,1))

```

## Least-cost path and cost corridor

Now that we have the cost surface, we can find the cheapest route from the source to the destination. `create_lcp()` finds the least-cost path, and `create_cost_corridor()` calculates, for every cell, the combined cost of the best route from the source to that cell and on to the destination. Cells with low values lie on or near a good route. To turn that surface into a corridor, we keep the cells whose cost is within 5% of the cheapest possible.

```{r lcp}
# least-cost path (the result is converted to a terra vector with vect())
lcp <- create_lcp(x = cs.6, origin = src.xy, destination = dest.xy,
                  cost_distance = TRUE, check_locations = TRUE)
lcp.vect <- vect(lcp)
as.data.frame(lcp.vect)          # includes the accumulated cost of the path

# length of the path, the straight-line distance between the two points, and the ratio
path.km <- sum(perim(lcp.vect)) / 1000
straight.km <- sqrt(sum((src.xy - dest.xy)^2)) / 1000
path.km
straight.km
path.km / straight.km
```
Take a moment to consider what that ratio of the LCP distance and the straight line distance represents. Was it very easy for your species to get from the source to the destination point? 


```{r corridor}
# cost corridor: keep cells within 5% of the cheapest possible cost
corridor <- create_cost_corridor(x = cs.6, origin = src.xy, destination = dest.xy)
min.cost <- global(corridor, "min", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1]
corridor.zone <- ifel(corridor <= min.cost * 1.05, 1, NA)

# How big is the corridor?
corridor.km2 <- global(corridor.zone, "notNA")[1, 1] * prod(res(current.proj)) / 1e6
corridor.km2
```

```{r lcp-map, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyterra)

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = future.proj) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "transparent", name = "Cost") +
  geom_spatvector(data = as.polygons(corridor.zone), fill = "red", alpha = 0.35, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_spatvector(data = lcp.vect, color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = as.data.frame(src.xy), aes(x = x, y = y), shape = 17, color = "blue", size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = as.data.frame(dest.xy), aes(x = x, y = y), shape = 15, color = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Least-cost path and corridor") +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(ext(lcp.vect)[1] * 0.95, ext(lcp.vect)[2] * 1.05), 
           ylim = c(ext(lcp.vect)[3] * 0.98, ext(lcp.vect)[4] * 1.02)) 
```

**A sanity check:** the path should mostly follow cells with higher suitability. If it cuts straight through the poorest habitat, check that you passed *conductance* (not resistance) to `create_cs()`.

## Adding human development

The SDM was built from climate alone, so it knows nothing about the things that most limit dispersal for many animals: roads, cities, and farmland. The **human footprint index** (Venter et al.) combines built-up areas, population density, power infrastructure, cropland, pasture, roads, railways, and waterways into a single score from 0 (low) to 50 (high pressure) at about 1 km resolution. Let's add it to the resistance surface.

The file is global, so the first download may take a few minutes. We crop it to your study region, project it onto the same grid as your resistance surface, and rescale it to 0-1. Then we **add** it to the resistance: the most heavily developed cells gain +100, making them as hard to cross as the worst natural habitat.

```{r footprint}
footprint <- geodata::footprint(year = 2009, path = "data")

fp <- crop(footprint, ext(current.suit))
fp.proj <- project(fp, current.proj, method = "average")   # average the finer cells within each coarser cell
fp.proj[is.na(fp.proj)] <- 0
fp.scaled <- clamp(fp.proj / 50, 0, 1)
plot(fp.scaled, main = "Human footprint (rescaled 0-1)")

resistance.hf <- resistance3 + 100 * fp.scaled
plot(resistance.hf, main = "Resistance (with HF)")
```

This weighting (+100) is an assumption for illustration. A different weight would change the result, and a real analysis would need to justify it. Now repeat the analysis with the new surface:

```{r lcp-hf}
cs.hf <- create_cs(x = 1 / resistance.hf, neighbours = 16)

lcp.hf <- create_lcp(x = cs.hf, origin = src.xy, destination = dest.xy,
                     cost_distance = TRUE, check_locations = TRUE)
lcp.hf.vect <- vect(lcp.hf)

corridor.hf <- create_cost_corridor(x = cs.hf, origin = src.xy, destination = dest.xy)
min.cost.hf <- global(corridor.hf, "min", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1]
corridor.hf.zone <- ifel(corridor.hf <= min.cost.hf * 1.05, 1, NA)

sum(perim(lcp.hf.vect)) / 1000       # length of the new path (km)
```

## Extra credit: all-pairs least-cost paths

So far we connected one source to one destination. Another approach (recall the factorial least-cost paths from lecture) is to calculate least-cost paths between *many* pairs of locations and then add them up, which shows where movement would concentrate across the landscape. The code below picks the best cell in each of your three largest current patches and your three largest gain patches., calculates the paths between all pairs, and combines them into a density map.

```{r extra-credit, eval = FALSE}
top.current <- head(patch.sizes$value[order(patch.sizes$count, decreasing = TRUE)], 3)
top.gain    <- head(gain.sizes$value[order(gain.sizes$count, decreasing = TRUE)], 3)

locs <- rbind(get.best.cells(current.patches, current.proj, top.current),
              get.best.cells(gain.patches, future.proj, top.gain))


```
